<a id="pm-s3"></a>
## 3. Proof roadmap

- **step-exact-cochains** [claim](#stmt-lem-cts-exact) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-cts-exact): Lift compact quotient cochain images and detect kernel continuity; use compact splitting and Artin–Rees for the stated coefficient cases. -> Exact continuous cochain sequences.
- **step-compact-resolution-comparison** [claim](#stmt-lem-cts-comparison) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-cts-comparison): Construct compact stable envelopes and compare compact bar resolutions with finite free completed resolutions. -> Resolution comparison and compact coefficient duality.
- **step-local-equivariant-sections** [claim](#stmt-lem-cts-local-section) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-cts-local-section): Correct a small nonabelian cocycle by convergent Lie-algebra averaging over the characteristic-zero field. -> Equivariant clopen local sections.
- **step-isotropy-vanishing** [claim](#stmt-prop-cts-isotropy-bound) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-cts-isotropy-bound): Tensor-induce a uniform-subgroup resolution and use trace splittings on finite isotropy pieces. -> A uniform cohomological bound preserved by finite twists.
- **step-full-group-duality** [claim](#stmt-prop-cts-full-duality) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-cts-full-duality): Retain orientation in uniform duality and show the finite quotient norm is an equivalence using bounded injective-projective models. -> Full-group homology-cohomology duality.
- **step-powered-division** [claim](#stmt-lem-mark-powered-division) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-mark-powered-division): Apply Weierstrass preparation and monic division to the powered coordinate; then check specialization and finite closure operations. -> Finite free powered division algebras and next-height compatibility.
- **step-connected-jet-model** [claim](#stmt-prop-mark-jets) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-mark-jets): Compare formal-group coefficients recursively and order residue monomials to obtain a triangular group action. -> Integral connected marking models with periodicity filtrations.
- **step-whole-marking-model** [claim](#stmt-prop-mark-whole-model) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-mark-whole-model): Tensor connected jets with the whole powered tuple algebra and select ordered étale bases by a localized invariant idempotent. -> Whole integral finite models and localized marking torsors.
- **step-root-lift-algebras** [claim](#stmt-prop-mark-roots) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-mark-roots): Use the division divisor to identify complete regular parameters, then compare finite free ranks to recover the full lift scheme. -> Natural root-algebra descriptions of generator lifts.
- **step-associated-coefficients** [claim](#stmt-lem-mark-associated-coefficients) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-mark-associated-coefficients): Split division groups using marked generator lifts and descend their finite-dimensional coordinate representations together with their maps. -> Finite translation representations at common finite marking levels.
- **step-geometric-trace** [claim](#stmt-prop-mark-finite-isotropy) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-mark-finite-isotropy): Contradict finite-order fixed points using growing connected division rank, and derive trace surjectivity by geometric freeness and Chinese remainders. -> Trace-one elements acting continuously on coefficient and support models.
- **step-boundary-strips** [claim](#stmt-lem-mark-strips) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-mark-strips): Filter each strip by conormal periodicity twists and pass to the countable union of strips with exact bounded-denominator cochains. -> Finite strip cohomology and countable localization defects.
- **step-honda-action** [claim](#stmt-lem-tower-honda-action) / [proof](#proof-stmt-thm-tower-comparison): Construct the covariant period series, verify relative continuity and scalar linearity, then apply relative full faithfulness. -> Composition-preserving Honda and bundle endomorphism comparison.
- **step-etale-tower** [claim](#stmt-lem-tower-etale-comparison) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-tower-etale-comparison): Normalize compatible division coordinates, prove uniform inverse estimates, and use the root closure coordinates for analytic surjectivity. -> Relative equivariant analytic identification of the étale tower.
- **step-full-tower-quotient** [claim](#stmt-thm-tower-comparison) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-tower-etale-comparison-2): Convert independent sections to relative subbundles, construct the connected quotient frame, and fix the determinant height to select integral frame torsors. -> The full marking quotient as independent extension tuples.
- **step-support-transport** [claim](#stmt-lem-tower-supports) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-tower-supports): Use quasi-compactness of compact torsors and their double bar complexes to transport cofinal support bounds. -> Equivariant support descent with retained bar parameters.
- **step-banach-limits** [claim](#stmt-lem-kum-banach-limits) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-kum-banach-limits): Solve finite difference strings with successively small corrections and take complete limits; approximate compact parameter functions by clopen constants. -> Vanishing derived-limit obstruction and termwise complex limits.
- **step-annular-homotopy** [claim](#stmt-prop-kum-annulus) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-kum-annulus): Diagonalize the Kummer difference operator on Laurent monomials and absorb inverse denominators using the prescribed radial gaps. -> A bounded uniform homotopy to the constant-monomial part.
- **step-line-disc-calculations** [claim](#stmt-prop-kum-line) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-kum-line): Kill the remaining annular class on a small disc, compute exterior germs, take support fibers, and iterate ordered coordinates. -> Relative ordinary, germ, and oriented compact-support comparisons.
- **step-low-graph-support** [claim](#stmt-lem-kum-low-support) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-kum-low-support): Use uniform child-to-parent support maps, finite descent filtrations, and the Milnor sequence to kill low-degree closed support. -> Pro-zero low-degree support systems and degree-zero deletion.
- **step-lattice-transitions** [claim](#stmt-lem-ind-lattice-transitions) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-ind-lattice-transitions): Compute lattice cohomology by the completed Koszul complex and reduce integral restriction and corestriction multipliers modulo the characteristic. -> Restriction and corestriction rules for lattice orientations.
- **step-whole-extension-support** [claim](#stmt-prop-ind-whole) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-ind-whole): Apply support Shapiro to translation-lattice bounds and take corestriction colimits after the geometric homotopies. -> Whole extension-space support comparison.
- **step-persistent-tubes** [claim](#stmt-prop-ind-tubes) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-ind-tubes): Obtain uniform norm equivalence from independence, choose persistent lattice gaps, and construct relative disc clusters with compatible collars. -> Cofinal uniform graph tubes at all depths.
- **step-rank-excision** [claim](#stmt-lem-ind-germ-excision) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-ind-germ-excision): Take exact support triangles on interleaved bounds and compute shrinking tube germs by restriction to shrinking lattice stabilizers. -> Rank deletion triangles with algebraic locally constant germ terms.
- **step-scalar-admissibility** [claim](#stmt-thm-ind-comparison) / [proof](#proof-stmt-thm-ind-comparison): Induct through rank deletion, glue finite slope partitions, derive smoothness from compact parameter comparison, and prove admissibility by parabolic induction. -> Scalar comparison and countable smooth admissible compact-support cohomology.
- **step-admissible-group-cohomology** [claim](#stmt-lem-ind-admissible-cohomology) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-ind-admissible-cohomology): Dualize to finitely generated compact modules and use finite free resolutions; retain uniform finite-span scalar families. -> Finite group cohomology and scalar-extension comparison.
- **step-finite-equivariant-support** [claim](#stmt-cor-ind-finite) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cor-ind-finite): Descend the compact frame torsors and take successive product-group cohomology with finite spectral-sequence diagonals. -> Finite equivariant geometric compact-support cohomology.
- **step-ordinary-functions** [claim](#stmt-cor-ind-functions) / [proof](#proof-stmt-cor-ind-functions): First take shrinking-support limits on a fixed output bound, then exhaust the output line; descend degree-zero sections through translations. -> Scalar ordinary functions and finite-field invariant algebraic functions.
- **step-root-functor** [claim](#stmt-prop-trans-roots) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-trans-roots): Use the power coaction on the total perfect lift torsor and associated-bundle induction in stages, retaining natural auxiliary actions. -> Natural coinduction-root comparison of exact diagrams.
- **step-invariant-volume** [claim](#stmt-prop-trans-volume) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-trans-volume): Descend a translation Lie frame, form its invariant volume, and compare torsor and Cartier dual generators through an invariant source unit. -> Invariant volume and finite-constant scalar normalization.
- **step-fixed-transfer** [claim](#stmt-prop-trans-cartier) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-trans-cartier): Normalize the Cartier operator, compose socle augmentations, establish the toral splitting in the multiplicative case, and bound fixed whole-basis matrices. -> One transfer with controlled iterates, stable lattice, and residue adjointness.
- **step-diagram-boundary-bound** [claim](#stmt-lem-trans-diagram-bound) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-trans-diagram-bound): Choose finite underlying module sections once and transport them through the entire root diagram. -> A fixed cocycle boundary operator with bounded pole loss.
- **step-laurent-supports** [claim](#stmt-prop-laurent-model) / [proof](#proof-stmt-prop-laurent-model): Split finite support restriction diagrams into Laurent parts, apply dense inverse-limit control, and solve coefficient Frobenius equations uniformly. -> Analytic and finite-field Laurent support models.
- **step-laurent-continuity** [claim](#stmt-lem-laurent-action) / [proof](#proof-stmt-lem-laurent-action): Factor integral coordinate changes, control output monomial weights, and combine finite basis matrices with dense finite-sum approximation. -> Jointly continuous group action and invertible absolute Frobenius.

<a id="pm-s4"></a>
## 4. Engineering Triptych

### Panel 1 - epistemic contract

- **invariant-free-rank-subset-count**: The free rank equals the number of subsets of the exterior generators whose degrees sum to the requested integer degree. The calculation determines the free rank independently of the prime.

### Panel 2 - negative knowledge

- **anti-use-rank-as-torsion-description**: Treat the computed free rank as a complete description of integral homotopy or as a calculation of its finite torsion summands. -> Distinct torsion summands can have the same free rank; the subset count contains no torsion multiplicities.
- **anti-use-arbitrary-invertible-spectrum**: Apply the sphere rank calculation and finite-generation conclusion to every invertible or dualizable local spectrum. -> The paper explicitly records invertible local spectra for which degreewise finite generation fails.
- **anti-use-finiteness-as-effective-termination**: Use the general finite-generation theorem as an effective stopping rule for recovering integral homotopy generators and torsion. -> Existence of finite invariants supplies neither a computable search cutoff nor a uniform bound on their size.

### Panel 3 - reference implementation and oracle

Applicability: `constructive`. The free-rank corollary gives a finite subset count for each fixed positive height and integer degree. This construction implements that corollary alone. It does not compute the general torsion summands or turn the continuous-cohomology finiteness proof into an algorithm.

```python
# INPUTS: A JSON object with integer fields n and j.
# PRECONDITIONS: 1 <= n <= 16; j is any integer; booleans are rejected.
# OUTPUTS: The exact free rank from the subset-count formula, as a JSON integer.
# TIME: O(n^3) exact integer additions; parsing also depends on input length.
# SPACE: O(n^2) integer counters, each with at most n+1 bits, plus input storage.
# ARITHMETIC: Arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic only.
# FAILURE: Invalid input raises an exception and exits unsuccessfully.
import json
import sys

obj = json.load(sys.stdin)
if not isinstance(obj, dict) or set(obj) != {'n', 'j'}:
    raise ValueError('expected exactly n and j')
n, j = obj['n'], obj['j']
if type(n) is not int or type(j) is not int or not 1 <= n <= 16:
    raise ValueError('invalid height or degree')
counts = {0: 1}
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    degree = 1 - 2 * i
    updated = counts.copy()
    for total, count in counts.items():
        updated[total + degree] = updated.get(total + degree, 0) + count
    counts = updated
answer = counts.get(j, 0)
print(json.dumps(answer))
```

## 6. Applicability limits and search

- **limit-finite-spectrum-scope** (counterexample_scope): The finite-spectrum conclusion does not extend to arbitrary invertible or dualizable local spectra. Blocked use: ['Apply degreewise finite generation to an arbitrary invertible or dualizable local spectrum solely from its invertibility or dualizability.']
- **limit-no-uniform-generator-torsion-bound** (formal_scope): Degreewise finite generation supplies no asserted uniform generator count or torsion order as the prime, height, or degree varies. Blocked use: ['Choose a uniform search cutoff for generators or torsion from the main theorem.']
- **limit-uncomputed-torsion-multiplicities** (unknown): The general torsion multiplicities remain undetermined by the finiteness proof. Blocked use: ['Report the free-rank calculation as a complete integral homotopy-group calculation.']
- **limit-no-fracture-map-calculation** (formal_scope): The proof does not compute chromatic fracture maps or finite torsion summands. Blocked use: ['Extract explicit fracture maps or splitting retractions from degreewise finite generation.']
- **limit-specified-continuous-cochains** (formal_scope): The coefficient assertions use the specified bounded-step continuous complex and actual algebraic images. Blocked use: ['Replace a boundary image by its closure.', 'Change the coefficient topology while retaining the same cohomology conclusions without a comparison proof.']
- **limit-exact-cochain-lifting** (hypothesis): Exactness of underlying coefficient spaces requires the stated kernel-continuity and compact-image lifting conditions before it gives exact continuous cochains. Blocked use: ['Infer exact continuous cochains from an arbitrary exact sequence of underlying vector spaces.']
- **limit-trace-and-orientation-duality** (hypothesis): Untwisted full-group duality requires trace admissibility and trivial orientation over the coefficient field. Blocked use: ['Apply the untwisted duality to arbitrary completed group-algebra modules.', 'Discard a nontrivial orientation line.']
- **limit-allowed-coefficient-class** (hypothesis): The coefficient theorem concerns the specified allowed class rather than arbitrary semilinear finite free modules. Blocked use: ['Extend coefficient finiteness to an arbitrary semilinear finite free module without proving membership in the allowed class.']
- **limit-whole-model-boundary** (formal_scope): Boundary arguments retain whole lattices before localization; the localized marking idempotent is not specialized across the closed locus. Blocked use: ['Assume the localized idempotent extends to the boundary and use its component as a whole finite free boundary model.']
- **limit-next-height-induction-input** (hypothesis): Boundary-strip finiteness and fixed-level open countability are conditional on coefficient finiteness at the next height. Blocked use: ['Use the open-stratum countability theorem as an unconditional input at an intermediate height.']
- **limit-finite-isotropy-marking-depth** (hypothesis): Geometric freeness and the resulting trace elements are established for torsion-free product marking subgroups. Blocked use: ['Apply the geometric trace construction at an arbitrary shallow marking level without its torsion-free hypothesis.']
- **limit-fixed-annulus** (edge_case): The narrowing homotopy compares different annuli after the prescribed radial change; it does not establish finite-dimensional cohomology for a fixed annulus. Blocked use: ['Infer fixed-annulus finite-dimensional cohomology from the annular restriction factorization.']
- **limit-untilted-versus-perfected-line** (formal_scope): The untilted affine-line calculation and the perfected characteristic-field Laurent calculation concern different spaces and different support computations. Blocked use: ['Transfer the affine-line support degree directly to the perfected Laurent domain.']
- **limit-distinct-support-directions** (formal_scope): Expanding supports, shrinking neighborhood germs, and support on an actual closed graph require their distinct maps and limit directions. Blocked use: ['Replace a neighborhood-germ colimit by an inverse limit of shrinking support fibers.', 'Infer ordinary algebraic-to-analytic cohomology comparison from the compact-support results.']
- **limit-uniform-graph-tube-hypotheses** (hypothesis): Closed-graph low-degree support vanishing requires cofinal graph tubes, uniform refinement ratios, separated collars, and admissible complement exhaustions on each fixed bound. Blocked use: ['Apply deletion invariance to an arbitrary closed analytic locus without verifying the graph-tube conditions.', 'Assume a common tube depth for every output bound.']
- **limit-parameter-ring-finiteness** (formal_scope): With an infinite compact profinite parameter retained, finiteness is over the continuous-function coefficient ring and does not mean finite dimension over the scalar field. Blocked use: ['Report parameter-dependent cohomology as finite-dimensional over the scalar field merely because it is finite over the parameter ring.']
- **limit-root-restriction-of-scalars** (formal_scope): The root-module convention includes restriction of scalars to the original marked ring; it does not preserve rank over that original ring. Blocked use: ['Treat a root bundle as having its original rank after restricting to the original coefficient ring.', 'Treat the translation power map as an automorphism onto the entire translation group.']
- **limit-auxiliary-actions-high-coinduction** (formal_scope): A common finite marking stage retains the natural auxiliary actions on high coinductions; simultaneous triviality of all those actions is not asserted. Blocked use: ['Replace all high coinduced marking actions by trivial actions after a single shrink.']
- **limit-height-one-transfer-branch** (edge_case): The positive-dimensional local distribution-ring argument requires the higher intermediate-height case; the multiplicative case instead uses the Cartier splitting of Frobenius. Blocked use: ['Apply the positive-dimensional top Koszul construction in the multiplicative-type case without its separate splitting argument.']
- **limit-distinct-frobenius-operators** (formal_scope): Coefficient-only Frobenius fixes monomial exponents, whereas absolute Frobenius scales them; coefficient descent and positive-order contraction use these different operations. Blocked use: ['Substitute coefficient-only Frobenius for the absolute Frobenius contraction of positive Laurent cycles.']
- **limit-nonconstructive-positive-acyclicity** (nonconstructive): Positive Laurent acyclicity uses analytic-subgroup openness and a contracting iterate; the proof supplies no effective bound for finding a primitive. Blocked use: ['Claim an executable general boundary search or a certified stopping time from the acyclicity proof.']
- **limit-stable-image-versus-localized-cohomology** (hypothesis): A finite compact stable image alone does not control all localized cohomology. The localized intersection argument also needs next-height finiteness and a countable consecutive transfer quotient. Blocked use: ['Deduce countability of all localized cohomology directly from finiteness of the compact stable image.', 'Assume the uniterated idempotent projection has countable kernel.']
- **limit-descent-vanishing-page** (hypothesis): The sphere descent argument requires strong convergence and a horizontal vanishing line at a finite page; it does not require finite cohomological dimension of the full stabilizer. Blocked use: ['Conclude finite homotopy merely from finite entries in an unbounded spectral sequence.', 'Replace the finite-page horizontal bound by an unsupported full-group cohomological-dimension claim.']

<a id="pm-s7"></a>
## 7. Complete mathematical paper


We prove that the homotopy groups of the $`K(n)`$-local sphere are finitely generated ℤ<sub><i>p</i></sub>-modules in every integer degree, for every prime <i>p</i> and positive height <i>n</i>. Equivalently, the same conclusion holds after $`K(n)`$-localizing any finite <i>p</i>-local spectrum. This answers the degreewise finiteness question of Hovey and Hovey–Strickland.

<a id="part:coefficients"></a>
### The finiteness problem and continuous coefficients

<a id="sec:introduction"></a>
##### Introduction

Let $p$ be a prime, let $K(n)$ denote Morava $K$-theory of height $n\geq 1$ at $p$, and let $S_p^\wedge$ be the $p$-completed sphere. Morava localization isolates a single chromatic height in stable homotopy theory. Even for the sphere, the localized spectrum is not connective, and a degreewise finiteness statement must control each integer degree without a connectivity assumption. The degreewise finite-generation question asks whether each of these groups is a finitely generated $\mathbb Z_p$-module. We prove that it is, at every prime and positive height.

<a id="stmt-thm-descent-integral"></a>
<div id="thm:descent-integral" class="theorem">

**Theorem 1**. *<span id="thm:main" label="thm:main"></span>For every prime $p$, every integer $n\geq 1$, and every integer $t$, the $\mathbb Z_p$-module $$\pi_t L_{K(n)}S_p^\wedge$$ is finitely generated. Equivalently, for every finite $p$-local spectrum $F$, the module $\pi_t L_{K(n)}F$ is finitely generated over $\mathbb Z_p$ in every integer degree $t$.*

</div>

The equivalence in the statement follows from finite cofiber sequences, suspensions, and retracts: finite generation over the Noetherian ring $\mathbb Z_p$ is preserved by kernels, cokernels, and extensions. The proof of the sphere assertion is completed in <a href="#sec:sphere" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:sphere">1</a>. There is no uniform bound asserted on the number of generators or on the order of the torsion as $p$, $n$, or $t$ varies.

<a id="sec:history"></a>
###### History and relation to earlier work

answers positively the degreewise finite-generation question stated by Hovey–Strickland (Hovey and Strickland 1999, Problem 16.2) <a id="pm-cite-1"></a>[[hoveyStrickland1999](#ref-hoveyStrickland1999)] and in Hovey’s Morava $K$- and $E$-theory problem list (Hovey n.d., Problem 1). In Li’s terminology, the question asks whether the local sphere is of *finite type*: its homotopy groups are finitely generated over $\mathbb Z_p$ in every integer degree (Li 2021, Introduction) <a id="pm-cite-2"></a>[[liFiniteType2021](#ref-liFiniteType2021)].

The classical height-one calculation expresses the local sphere as the fiber of an Adams operation on completed $K$-theory (Hopkins 2014, secs. 1–2) <a id="pm-cite-3"></a>[[hopkinsKOne](#ref-hopkinsKOne)]; we recall the all-degree answer at odd primes in <a href="#prop:sphere-height-one" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:sphere-height-one">67</a>. At height two and $p\geq5$, Hovey–Strickland’s analysis of Shimomura’s calculations proves that $\pi_aL_{K(2)}F$ is finite for every finite torsion spectrum $F$ and every integer $a$ (Hovey and Strickland 1999, sec. 15.2 and Theorem 15.1) <a id="pm-cite-4"></a>[[hoveyStrickland1999](#ref-hoveyStrickland1999)]. Applied to the Moore spectrum, this supplies the mod-$p$ finiteness criterion for the sphere in that range. The proof here establishes that criterion uniformly in the prime and height.

Devinatz approached integral finiteness through continuous homotopy fixed points for smaller subgroups of the Morava stabilizer. He used *essentially finite rank*, a condition of finite generation over the periodicity ring after quotienting by the closure of periodicity torsion (Devinatz 2007, sec. 4) <a id="pm-cite-5"></a>[[devinatzHomotopy2007](#ref-devinatzHomotopy2007)]. For Morava $E$-theory $E_n$ and certain closed procyclic stabilizer subgroups $H$, he proved this property for $\pi_*(E_n^{hH}\wedge F)$ under chromatic-acyclicity and annihilation hypotheses on the finite spectrum $F$ (Devinatz 2008) <a id="pm-cite-6"></a>[[devinatzFiniteness2008](#ref-devinatzFiniteness2008)]. Such intermediate fixed-point spectra require their own finiteness condition; these results are distinct from degreewise finite generation for the full local sphere.

Barthel–Schlank–Stapleton–Weinstein determined the rational answer at every prime and height (Barthel et al. 2025, Theorem A) <a id="pm-cite-7"></a>[[bssw2024](#ref-bssw2024)]: $$\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\pi_*L_{K(n)}S
 \cong \Lambda_{\mathbb Q_p}(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_n),
 \qquad |\zeta_i|=1-2i.$$ Their coefficient comparison also gives a split injection from Witt-vector cohomology into degree-zero Lubin–Tate coefficient cohomology whose complement in each cohomological degree is killed by a power of $p$ (Barthel et al. 2025, Theorem B) <a id="pm-cite-8"></a>[[bssw2024](#ref-bssw2024)]. These conclusions do not bound the size of integral torsion: the compact module $\prod_{j\geq1}\mathbb F_p$ has zero rationalization and exponent $p$, but is not finitely generated over $\mathbb Z_p$. The present theorem proves that the torsion subgroup is finite in each integer homotopy degree. Combined with the rational calculation, it determines the free ranks in <a href="#cor:sphere-ranks" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="cor:sphere-ranks">66</a>.

Continuous Morava descent links coefficient cohomology to sphere homotopy (Devinatz and Hopkins 2004, Theorem 1 and Appendix A) <a id="pm-cite-9"></a>[[devinatzHopkins2004](#ref-devinatzHopkins2004)]. The Hopkins–Ravenel smash product theorem, in the descendability formulation of Mathew, gives a horizontal vanishing line at a finite page (Mathew 2016, Corollary 4.4, Theorem 4.18 and Proposition 10.10) <a id="pm-cite-10"></a>[[mathew2016](#ref-mathew2016)]. Heard states the resulting strongly convergent local Adams spectral sequence at every prime and height, with a finite-page bound independent of the input spectrum (Heard 2023, Theorem 4.6 and Proposition 4.13) <a id="pm-cite-11"></a>[[heard2023](#ref-heard2023)]. Consequently, finite coefficient cohomology for the Moore spectrum is enough to obtain finite homotopy in each degree. Establishing that coefficient finiteness is the main task of this paper.

Our geometric argument places Lubin–Tate deformation theory and Strauch’s torsion strata (Lubin and Tate 1966; Strauch 2007) <a id="pm-cite-12"></a>[[lubinTate1966](#ref-lubinTate1966), [strauch2007](#ref-strauch2007)] in the geometry of the Fargues–Fontaine curve (Fargues and Fontaine 2018) <a id="pm-cite-13"></a>[[farguesFontaine2018](#ref-farguesFontaine2018)]. Scholze–Weinstein relate $p$-divisible groups and their universal covers to sections of associated bundles (Scholze and Weinstein 2013) <a id="pm-cite-14"></a>[[scholzeWeinstein2013](#ref-scholzeWeinstein2013)]; the relative bundle and cohomology results used here are those of Fargues–Scholze (Fargues and Scholze 2026) <a id="pm-cite-15"></a>[[farguesScholze2021](#ref-farguesScholze2021)]. The Banach–Colmez theory initiated by Colmez (Colmez 2002) <a id="pm-cite-16"></a>[[colmez2002](#ref-colmez2002)] was related to coherent sheaves on the curve by Le Bras (Le Bras 2018) <a id="pm-cite-17"></a>[[lebras2018](#ref-lebras2018)]. Anschütz–Le Bras’s relative full-faithfulness theorem supplies the passage from the compatible linear morphisms of section sheaves constructed below to bundle maps in families (Anschütz and Le Bras 2025, Corollary 3.11) <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[anschutzLeBras2025](#ref-anschutzLeBras2025)]. Within this framework, [sec:completed-tower,sec:kummer,sec:independent-tuples] [sec:completed-tower](#sec:completed-tower), [sec:kummer](#sec:kummer), [sec:independent-tuples](#sec:independent-tuples) construct the marked quotient on each height stratum and its compact-support comparisons, retaining the marking actions and the directions of the support limits.

The passage from geometric supports back to compact coefficients also uses analytic-group duality. Lazard’s theory and the formulation of Beaudry–Goerss–Hopkins–Stojanoska provide the uniform-subgroup resolutions and their orientation data (Lazard 1965; Beaudry et al. 2022) <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[lazard1965](#ref-lazard1965), [bghs](#ref-bghs)]. The tensor-induction method, recalled by Symonds in its profinite form, passes from an open subgroup to a complex with finite isotropy (Symonds 2007, Theorem 5.2) <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[symonds2007](#ref-symonds2007)]. In <a href="#sec:continuous" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:continuous">2</a>, trace-one elements for these finite stabilizers replace averaging by their orders. This permits the complete-step coefficient comparisons and full-group norm argument even when the stabilizer has $p$-torsion.

The transfer argument combines classical constructions with a uniformity problem at finite marking level. Cartier’s $p$-basis construction identifies differential forms with Frobenius-twisted de Rham cohomology (Cartier 1957, sec. 3, Theorem 1) <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[cartier1957](#ref-cartier1957)]; we use the inverse-linear operator in the conventions of Blickle–Böckle (Blickle and Böckle 2011, Definition 2.1 and Example 2.23) <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[blickleBockle2011](#ref-blickleBockle2011)]. Lipman’s formal residue transformation law gives the finite-root comparison (Lipman 1984, Lemmas (7.2)(b) and (7.3)) <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[lipmanResidues1984](#ref-lipmanResidues1984)]. The additional work is to control the poles of all transfer iterates and to choose one finite marking level for all sufficiently high transfers. These are the steps that return the geometric finiteness statement to the compact coefficient modules ([sec:transfers,sec:laurent,sec:cutoff,sec:pro-transfer] [sec:transfers](#sec:transfers), [sec:laurent](#sec:laurent), [sec:cutoff](#sec:cutoff), [sec:pro-transfer](#sec:pro-transfer)).

Degreewise finite generation does not extend to every invertible $K(n)$-local spectrum. At height two and $p\geq5$, Hovey–Strickland’s analysis of $p$-adically graded spheres gives invertible spectra that are not of finite type (Hovey and Strickland 1999, Theorem 15.1) <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[hoveyStrickland1999](#ref-hoveyStrickland1999)]; Li classifies the finite-type invertibles in this range (Li 2021, Theorem 4.22) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[liFiniteType2021](#ref-liFiniteType2021)]. Thus arbitrary invertible or dualizable local spectra cannot replace the finite spectra in <a href="#thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="thm:main">[thm:main]</a>. The proof makes no chromatic splitting assumption, and it does not compute the finite torsion summands or the chromatic fracture maps.

<a id="pm-h-5"></a>
###### The coefficient theorem

Fix a height $n$ formal group over a sufficiently large finite field $k$ of characteristic $p$. Let $E_n$ be its Morava $E$-theory and let $P_n$ be its ordinary stabilizer group. The algebraic conclusion that drives the proof is <a id="eq:intro-coefficients"></a>$$\label{eq:intro-coefficients}
 H^a_{\mathrm{cts}}\bigl(P_n;(E_n)_{2t}/p\bigr)
 \quad\text{is finite for every }a\geq0\text{ and }t\in\mathbb Z.$$ Here the coefficients have their compact deformation-parameter topology. The proof retains a precise larger class: integer powers of the periodicity line tensored with functions on whole finite tuples of division points, with specified Frobenius-powered coordinates, and finite sums, tensor products, equivariant summands, and finite filtrations of these modules. Its exact definition is <a href="#def:mark-coefficients" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="def:mark-coefficients">10</a>; its finiteness theorem and Morava consequence are [thm:coeff-finite,cor:coeff-morava]. Using whole division-point schemes allows restriction to a deeper height stratum and descent through finite marking covers. The assertion is about this class, rather than arbitrary semilinear finite free modules.

Here is why this coefficient theorem suffices for the sphere. The finite Galois quotient from $P_n$ to the extended stabilizer $\mathbb G_n$ preserves degreewise finiteness, including when its order is divisible by $p$. Morava descent for the Moore spectrum $S/p$ then has finite second-page entries. A horizontal vanishing line on a finite page leaves only finitely many of them in each limiting stem, so $\pi_*L_{K(n)}(S/p)$ is finite in each degree. Finally, positive-height locality gives derived $p$-completeness. The finite $p$-power cofibers present each integral homotopy group as a compact $\mathbb Z_p$-module with finite quotient modulo $p$; compact Nakayama proves finite generation. These steps are proved in <a href="#sec:sphere" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:sphere">1</a>. The horizontal bound concerns a later page of the descent spectral sequence; finite mod-$p$ cohomological dimension of the full stabilizer is not needed.

<a id="pm-h-6"></a>
###### The open-stratum argument

Write $$A_m=k[[u_m,\ldots,u_{n-1}]],\qquad
 B_m=A_m[u_m^{-1}]\quad(1\leq m<n),\qquad A_n=k.$$ We prove coefficient finiteness by downward induction from $A_n$. At the step indexed by $m$, put $x=u_m$ and $G=P_n$. The next-height hypothesis makes the cohomology of every finite boundary strip $x^aM/x^bM$ finite. Thus localization from a compact allowed coefficient $M$ to $M[1/x]$ has countable kernel and cokernel on cohomology. It remains to prove that open-stratum cohomology is countable: the original coefficient cohomology will then be compact Hausdorff and countable, hence finite. This explains why an intermediate countability theorem can prove a finiteness theorem.

We work first on finite covers $B_U$ of $B_m$ that mark the connected formal group and the étale Tate module. The index $U$ is an open subgroup of the two marking groups. The finite cover is an idempotent summand of a localized whole finite free model $A'[1/x]$. Keeping the whole model before localization ensures that its boundary layers remain in the next-height coefficient class. For a suitable compact lattice $\mathcal P=x^{-D}A'$, set $$M^i_U=H^i_\mathrm{cts}(G,\mathcal P),\qquad
 X^i_U=H^i_\mathrm{cts}(G,B_U).$$ The central task is countability of $X^i_U$ at every sufficiently deep *fixed* marking level. A statement only after taking the union of all marking levels would not suffice for the return to compact coefficients.

The completed marking tower provides the geometric input. Its quotient by $G$ is the space of independent $r$-tuples in $H^1(\mathcal O(-1/m))$ on the relative Fargues–Fontaine curve, where $\mathcal O(-1/m)$ has rank $m$ and degree $-1$, and $r=n-m$. Uniform Kummer calculations and deletion of dependent tuples make the equivariant compact-support cohomology finite. A separate ordinary-function calculation shows that invariant algebraic functions on the tower are constants. This permits a single normalization of a Cartier transfer $S$ on $B_U$ at one finite marking stage. Its pole estimate divides the pole order by a fixed power of $p$, up to a fixed additive loss; consequently $\mathcal P$ can be chosen $S$-stable and eventually contains the transfer iterates of every bounded-pole lattice.

To use the compact-support result, we express it as a Laurent module $W$ of convergent series with fractional $p$-power exponents, for which every $H_i(G,W)$ is finite over $k$. Residues identify its quotient by the subspace $W_+$ of positive-$x$-order series with the discrete transpose transfer tower: $$W/W_+\simeq
 \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}\bigl(\mathcal P^\vee\xrightarrow{S^\vee}
                   \mathcal P^\vee\xrightarrow{S^\vee}\cdots\bigr).$$ Here $\mathcal P^\vee$ is the continuous $k$-linear dual. The positive-order kernel is homologically acyclic. Its homology is countable; an analytic-subgroup argument using the Baire property then makes boundaries open in each complete cycle space, and absolute Frobenius contracts each positive-order cycle into that open subgroup. Invertibility of Frobenius then makes the original cycle a boundary. Compact duality gives $$I^i_U=\bigcap_{a\geq0}S^aM^i_U\quad\text{finite}.$$ Thus geometry controls a stable transfer image. It has not yet controlled all of $X^i_U$.

The remaining argument uses the finite translation representations of the generator-lift torsor. For $m>1$ their distribution algebra is the regular local ring $\Lambda=k[[D_1,\ldots,D_d]]$, with $d=(m-1)r$. Exact pro-completion first shows that consecutive transfer images stabilize modulo countable spaces on a marking tail. Together with the next-height boundary comparison, this upgrades the compact result to finiteness of $$F^i_U=\bigcap_{a\geq0}
       \mathop{\mathrm{im}}\bigl(S^aM^i_U\longrightarrow X^i_U\bigr).$$ Suppose some $X^i_U$ remained uncountable at arbitrarily deep levels, and choose the highest such degree $b$; the finite-isotropy bound makes this possible. A top Koszul extension then gives a finite-diagram operation from degree $b-d$ on a fixed root cover to degree $b$ on $B_U$, with countable cokernel. One common marking shrink makes that operation factor through every sufficiently high transfer. These factorizations use coinduced diagrams of one fixed self-extension, whose boundary operator has bounded pole loss. Modulo a countable quotient, the source classes of the top operation have positive-order cocycle representatives. Powering these representatives eventually absorbs that pole loss, so their images belong to every late compact transfer image and hence to $F^b_U$. The operation therefore has countable image as well as countable cokernel, contradicting the choice of $b$. For $m=1$, a Cartier splitting of Frobenius replaces the top extension and gives the same conclusion directly.

This is the bridge from geometric finiteness to ordinary coefficient cohomology. [sec:finite-markings](#sec:finite-markings), [sec:completed-tower](#sec:completed-tower) construct the finite models and identify the tower; [sec:kummer,sec:independent-tuples] [sec:kummer](#sec:kummer), [sec:independent-tuples](#sec:independent-tuples) prove its two geometric outputs. The transfer and Laurent models are developed in [sec:transfers,sec:laurent] [sec:transfers](#sec:transfers), [sec:laurent](#sec:laurent), and [sec:cutoff,sec:pro-transfer] [sec:cutoff](#sec:cutoff), [sec:pro-transfer](#sec:pro-transfer) prove the stable-image and fixed-level countability assertions just described. [sec:coefficients](#sec:coefficients) extends countability to the allowed coefficient class, descends the finite marking cover, and closes the height induction. The continuous-cochain framework used throughout is established first in <a href="#sec:continuous" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:continuous">2</a>.

The geometric completion enters through compact supports and the transpose transfer tower. Compact supports, neighborhood germs, and supports shrinking to a closed locus use different directions of passage; <a href="#fig:support-directions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="fig:support-directions">1</a> displays their maps and the cohomology that survives. These distinctions permit the argument to return to an individual algebraic marking level.

<a id="pm-h-7"></a>
###### Conventions

Throughout the coefficient argument, $k$ is finite. It may be enlarged by a finite extension to define the Honda models and their endomorphisms. We write $G=P_n$ and reserve $\mathbb G_n$ for the extended stabilizer in <a href="#sec:sphere" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:sphere">1</a>. All group cohomology is continuous, with the topological coefficient conventions of <a href="#sec:continuous" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:continuous">2</a>. Compact lattices carry their adic topology; localized coefficients use continuous cochains with a bounded denominator. Group homology is denoted by $H_i$ and cohomology by $H^i$.

For analytic arguments, $C=\mathbb C_p$ and $C^\flat$ is its tilt. If $\mathcal D$ is a compact profinite parameter space, write $R_{\mathcal D}=C(\mathcal D,C^\flat)$ for its continuous-function ring. Statements of finiteness with parameters mean finiteness over $R_{\mathcal D}$. The coefficient-only Frobenius $\varphi$ fixes monomial exponents; the absolute Frobenius $\mathop{\mathrm{Fr}}$ also scales them. These two operations are distinguished throughout.

We use cohomological grading for complexes. A limit over shrinking supports, a colimit of restrictions defining a germ, and a colimit of corestrictions over expanding supports are specified separately whenever they occur.

<a id="pm-h-8"></a>
##### Continuous coefficients and full-group duality

The coefficient modules below include compact formal lattices, their localizations, and spaces of convergent Laurent series. We first specify one cochain convention that applies to all three. Finite free resolution terms make the cohomology of compact coefficients compact Hausdorff; this is the input used when countability is upgraded to finiteness. The marked Laurent support module needs a second conclusion: duality between its group homology and cohomology for the full ordinary stabilizer. For that module, trace-one elements for finite subgroups replace averaging by their orders and permit the full-group duality argument below. The two conclusions have different hypotheses; only the second requires the trace condition. In this section $k$ is a finite field of characteristic $p$, and $G$ is a compact $p$-adic analytic group.

<a id="stmt-def-cts-steps"></a>
<div id="def:cts-steps" class="definition">

**Definition 2** (Complete steps). A coefficient module with complete steps is a vector space $M=\bigcup_{a\geq 0}M_a$, where the $M_a$ are complete Hausdorff linearly topologized $k$-spaces and the inclusions are continuous injections. The inclusions need not induce the topology on the smaller space. An action of $G$ is required to have the following property: for every $a$ there is a $b$ for which $G M_a\subset M_b$ and $G\times M_a\longrightarrow M_b$ is continuous. Morphisms satisfy the analogous condition with no group variable. We use the bounded-step continuous cochains $$C^j_{\mathrm{cts}}(G,M)=\mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_a C_{\mathrm{cts}}(G^j,M_a)$$ with the usual inhomogeneous differential. Their cohomology is denoted $H^j(G,M)$. The same convention applies to continuous functions on any compact profinite parameter space $\mathcal D$: its complete steps are $C_{\mathrm{cts}}(\mathcal D,M_a)$ with the topology of uniform convergence.

</div>

All subsequent assertions about these coefficient modules refer to this specified complex; they do not replace an algebraic image by its closure. Finite-dimensional discrete modules and compact modules are special cases. A localization of a finite module over $k[[x,y_1,\ldots,y_s]]$ has the steps $x^{-a}M_0$, with their adic topologies. Laurent modules have the complete steps specified in <a href="#sec:laurent" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:laurent">2</a>.

<a id="stmt-lem-cts-exact"></a>
<div id="lem:cts-exact" class="lemma">

**Lemma 3** (Exact cochains). *Consider an exact sequence of underlying vector spaces $$0\longrightarrow M'\xrightarrow{\iota}M\xrightarrow{q}M''
 \longrightarrow0$$ whose maps and actions respect complete steps. Suppose that:*

1.  *a bounded-step continuous map from a compact profinite space to $M$ with image in $\iota(M')$ is bounded-step continuous as a map to $M'$;*

2.  *for every compact subset $T$ of a step of $M''$, there is a continuous map $s:T\to M_b$ into one step of $M$, with $qs=\mathop{\mathrm{id}}_T$.*

*Then the corresponding sequence of continuous cochain complexes is short exact. In particular, it has the usual long exact cohomology sequence. These hypotheses hold for strict short exact sequences of compact $k$-spaces, for short exact sequences of finite modules over a complete Noetherian local $k$-algebra with finite residue field, and for their localizations with the lattice steps just described.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cts-exact"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cts-exact</summary>

*Proof.* The kernel assertion is (i). A cochain in the quotient has compact image $T$ in a single step, and composing it with the section in (ii) lifts that cochain. The section is not required to commute with $G$. Thus every degree of the cochain sequence is exact.

For compact vector spaces, continuous duality with discrete vector spaces turns a strict surjection into an injection. Splitting that injection as a map of vector spaces and dualizing gives a continuous $k$-linear section. In the Noetherian local case the modules are compact. A submodule is closed, and its induced topology is its adic topology by Artin–Rees. This proves (i), while the compact splitting proves (ii). For a localization, a fixed quotient lattice is the image of a compact source lattice: choose lifts of finitely many module generators and a common denominator. Its map from that source lattice is a strict compact surjection and has a continuous linear section. The kernel in a fixed lattice is again a finite module, so Artin–Rees gives (i) after a common enlargement of the denominator. This also proves the assertions for finite twists and finite direct sums. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-cts-comparison"></a>
<div id="lem:cts-comparison" class="lemma">

**Lemma 4** (Compact envelopes and comparison). *Let $M$ satisfy <a href="#def:cts-steps" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="def:cts-steps">2</a>.*

1.  *Every compact subset of a step of $M$ is contained in a compact $G$-stable $k$-subspace $N$ lying in one complete step. The action on $N$ is continuous. These $N$ form a filtered system whose union is $M$, and $$C^\bullet_{\mathrm{cts}}(G,M)
           =\mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_N C^\bullet_{\mathrm{cts}}(G,N).$$*

2.  *The ring $k[[G]]$ is Noetherian, and the trivial compact module $k$ has a resolution $P_\bullet$ by finitely generated free compact $k[[G]]$-modules. It may be unbounded. The comparison map $$\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{k[[G]],\mathrm{cts}}(P_\bullet,M)
              \simeq C^\bullet_{\mathrm{cts}}(G,M)$$ is a natural quasi-isomorphism. Every term on the left is a finite power of $M$.*

3.  *A right resolution by finitely generated free compact modules similarly defines $H_i(G,M)$. For compact $M$, cohomology and homology computed this way are compact Hausdorff, and continuous duality interchanges homology and cohomology, with the contragredient action on $M^\vee=\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{\mathrm{cts}}(M,k)$.*

*For $G=\mathbb Z_p$ with generator $\gamma$, the cochain complex is $[M\xrightarrow{\gamma-1}M]$ in degrees $0,1$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cts-comparison"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cts-comparison</summary>

*Proof.* Let $T\subset M_a$ be compact. The set $GT$ is compact in some $M_b$. Let $N$ be its closed linear span there. Modulo any open linear subspace of $M_b$, the image of $GT$ is finite. Since $k$ is finite, its linear span in that discrete quotient is finite as well. Thus $N$ is totally bounded and complete, hence compact. For any $g\in G$, the action map $M_b\to M_c$ is continuous after enlarging $c$ uniformly in $g$. The image of $N$ in the Hausdorff space $M_c$ is compact and closed. It contains the image of the linear span of $GT$, and continuity therefore shows $gN\subset N$. The injection $N\to M_c$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, so the restricted action is continuous. A finite sum of such spaces is again compact in a common step. Every element, and every compact cochain image, is contained in one of them. A map from a compact domain whose image lies in $N$ is continuous into $N$, by its subspace topology in $M_b$. This proves (i), including the assertion about cochains.

Choose a normal uniform open subgroup $K\subset G$. For the augmentation filtration of $k[[K]]$, the associated graded ring is a polynomial ring on $\dim G$ variables. Thus $k[[K]]$ is Noetherian, and the finite crossed-product extension $k[[G]]$ is Noetherian as well. Successively resolving the finitely generated kernels of a finite free presentation gives $P_\bullet$. For a compact module $N$, compare it with the compact bar resolution. Its terms are induced from compact $k$-spaces and are projective: every compact $k$-space is projective by continuous linear duality, and completed induction preserves that lifting property. Both are projective resolutions, and their augmentations and acyclic kernels split as compact $k$-spaces by continuous duality. The lifting construction for resolutions gives chain maps and chain homotopies in the compact category. Applying continuous Hom gives the usual continuous bar cochains. For comparison with the ind-profinite formulation under its countability hypotheses, see Boggi and Corob Cook (2016, Proposition 8.2 and Corollary 8.4) <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[boggiCorobCook](#ref-boggiCorobCook)]. The compact splitting argument just given does not impose second countability on $N$ and proves that all its comparison homotopies are continuous.

There is a well-defined $k[[G]]$-action on $M$: integrate on a compact $G$-stable envelope of a given element. It is independent of that envelope. Since every $P_j$ is finite free, its Hom into $M$ is the filtered union of its Hom into the $N$. Filtered colimits of vector spaces are exact. Passing the compact comparison and its homotopies through this colimit proves (ii); in particular no new completion is introduced. The same argument applies to the finite free right resolution and tensor products. For compact $N$, every differential has compact, hence closed, image in a finite power of $N$. Continuous duality is exact on compact vector spaces and takes these finite-power complexes to the corresponding dual complexes. This proves (iii). Finally, $k[[\mathbb Z_p]]=k[[\gamma-1]]$, and multiplication by $\gamma-1$ gives the stated two-term free resolution. ◻

</details>

We next make the finite-isotropy hypothesis explicit. Its verification for the geometric coefficient algebras will be given in <a href="#prop:mark-finite-isotropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:mark-finite-isotropy">16</a>.

<a id="stmt-def-cts-trace"></a>
<div id="def:cts-trace" class="definition">

**Definition 5** (Trace elements). Let $A$ be a commutative $k$-algebra with a $G$-action. A semilinear $A$-module $M$ with complete steps is trace-admissible if, for every finite subgroup $F\subset G$, there is $t_F\in A$ satisfying $$\sum_{f\in F}f(t_F)=1,$$ and multiplication by $t_F$ carries each complete step continuously into some complete step. The action is semilinear in the sense that $g(am)=g(a)g(m)$.

</div>

We will need an elementary local fact about the finite stabilizers of profinite spaces. The characteristic-zero Lie group in its proof is the group $K$, even though the coefficient field has characteristic $p$.

<a id="stmt-lem-cts-local-section"></a>
<div id="lem:cts-local-section" class="lemma">

**Lemma 6** (Equivariant local sections). *Let $K$ be a normal uniform open subgroup of $G$, and let $X$ be a profinite $G$-space on which $K$ acts freely. Suppose that $X\to Y=K\backslash X$ has a continuous $K$-equivariant trivialization as a principal $K$-space. Put $H=G/K$. If $x\in X$ and $y$ is its image, the finite group $G_x$ maps isomorphically to $H_y$. There is an $H_y$-invariant clopen neighborhood $V$ of $y$ and a section $s:V\to X$, with $s(y)=x$, which is equivariant for $G_x\simeq H_y$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cts-local-section"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cts-local-section</summary>

*Proof.* An element of $H_y$ has a lift taking $x$ into its $K$-orbit. Correcting that lift by the unique element of $K$ gives an element fixing $x$. Since $K$ acts freely, the resulting homomorphism $G_x\to H_y$ is bijective. Write $F=G_x$. A continuous section with value $x$ at $y$ exists by the assumed trivialization. Its failure to be $F$-equivariant is a continuous nonabelian cocycle $c_f\in C(V,K)$ for the action combining conjugation by $F$ and its action on $V$. All $c_f(y)$ equal $1$. Shrinking to an $F$-invariant clopen neighborhood makes all these cocycles arbitrarily close to $1$.

Here is the required small-cocycle argument, including the case $p\mid |F|$. Choose an $F$-stable sufficiently small Lie lattice in $\mathop{\mathrm{Lie}}(K)$ on which exponential, logarithm, and the Campbell–Hausdorff formula converge. In the Banach space of continuous functions on $V$ with values in $\mathop{\mathrm{Lie}}(K)$, use the supremum norm of an $F$-invariant norm. Put $\lambda_f=\log c_f$ and $\epsilon=\max_f\|\lambda_f\|$. Convergence of the Campbell–Hausdorff series gives, for a fixed constant $c$, the bound $$\|\lambda_{fg}-\lambda_f-f\lambda_g\|\leq c\epsilon^2.$$ With $b=|F|^{-1}\sum_f\lambda_f$, summing this identity over $g$ gives $$\|\lambda_f+fb-b\|\leq c|\,|F|\,|_p^{-1}\epsilon^2,
 \qquad \|b\|\leq |\,|F|\,|_p^{-1}\epsilon.$$ Changing the section by $\exp(-b)$ changes its cocycle to $\exp(-b)c_f f(\exp b)$. Another application of the same convergence estimate bounds the new logarithms by $c'\epsilon^2$, for a constant $c'$ depending only on $F$ and the chosen Lie lattice. Choose the initial neighborhood small enough that these exponentials stay in the convergence lattice and $c'\epsilon<1$. Iteration then gives uniformly convergent continuous changes of section, since the successive logarithms tend to zero at least quadratically. The limit has trivial cocycle. Every change is the identity at $y$, so the limiting section still takes $y$ to $x$. Division by $|F|$ was only performed in $\mathbb Q_p$; its fixed norm loss was absorbed in the initial choice of neighborhood. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-prop-cts-isotropy-bound"></a>
<div id="prop:cts-isotropy-bound" class="proposition">

**Proposition 7** (A uniform finite-isotropy bound). *Fix a normal uniform open subgroup $K\subset G$, and put $d_G=\dim G$ and $a_G=[G:K]$. If $M$ is trace-admissible, then $$H^j(G,M)=0\qquad(j>a_Gd_G).$$ The same bound holds for $M\otimes_kV$ for every finite-dimensional continuous $G$-representation $V$. Neither the bound nor the choice of $K$ depends on $M$ or $V$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-cts-isotropy-bound"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-cts-isotropy-bound</summary>

*Proof.* First consider a finite subgroup $F$ and a semilinear module $L$ with a trace element $t=t_F$. The map $$L\longrightarrow k[F]\otimes_kL,
 \qquad v\longmapsto\sum_{f\in F}f\otimes t f^{-1}v$$ is $F$-linear when $F$ acts on the first factor of the target. Its composite with $f\otimes v\mapsto fv$ is multiplication by $\sum_f f(t)=1$. Thus $L$ is a direct summand of an induced module. The same formulas on continuous cochains, which are finite sums of bounded continuous operators, show $H^{>0}(F,L)=0$ in our convention. They apply also to continuous function modules with pointwise multiplication by $t$, and to any finite-dimensional twist.

The trivial $k[[K]]$-module has a finite free resolution of length $d_G$. For finite cohomological dimension and uniform-group Poincare duality, see Lazard (1965, chap. V, Proposition 2.5.7.1 and Theorem 2.5.8) <a id="pm-cite-27"></a>[[lazard1965](#ref-lazard1965)] and Beaudry et al. (2022, Lemma 4.15 and Proposition 4.16) <a id="pm-cite-28"></a>[[bghs](#ref-bghs)]. Thus $k$ has projective dimension $d_G$, and the Noetherian local ring $k[[K]]$ has finitely generated free terms in a minimal resolution. A sufficiently deep uniform subgroup is used also when $p=2$. Tensor-induce this resolution from $K$ to $G$: take its completed tensor product over the $a_G$ cosets and let $G$ permute the factors, using the usual signs of complexes and the conjugate $K$-actions. Denote the resulting augmented complex by $T_\bullet\to k$. It is concentrated in degrees $0$ through $a_Gd_G$. The original augmented resolution is split exact as a complex of compact $k$-spaces. Its tensor product is therefore again a split resolution of $k$ in that category. This is the tensor-induction construction of Symonds (2007, Theorem 5.2) <a id="pm-cite-29"></a>[[symonds2007](#ref-symonds2007)].

<a id="eq:cts-permutation-acyclic"></a>
Each term of $T_\bullet$ is a finite sum of signed permutation modules $k[[X]]$. Here $X$ is a finite disjoint union of products of copies of $K$, one for each tensor factor. The diagonal $K$-action is free, and setting the first coordinate equal to $1$ gives a continuous trivialization of $X\to K\backslash X$. A possible sign is a locally constant rank-one coefficient and will be carried along. We claim that $$H^j\bigl(G,\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{k,\mathrm{cts}}(k[[X]],M)\bigr)=0\quad(j>0).
 \label{eq:cts-permutation-acyclic}$$ The Hom module is $C_{\mathrm{cts}}(X,M)$, with complete uniform-convergence steps. A $K$-trivialization identifies it, after untwisting the diagonal action on $M$, with a continuously coinduced $K$-module. Evaluation in the first coordinate contracts the coinduced bar complex, so its positive $K$-cohomology vanishes. All operators in that contraction are bounded continuous operators on function steps. The Hochschild–Serre double complex therefore reduces its $G$-cohomology to the cohomology of $H=G/K$ on the $K$-invariants.

Apply <a href="#lem:cts-local-section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cts-local-section">6</a> at a point of $Y=K\backslash X$. After shrinking its neighborhood $V$ further, its translates by elements outside $H_y$ are disjoint: first separate $y$ from the finitely many distinct points $hy$, and then intersect the resulting clopen neighborhoods. On the induced neighborhood $HV$, the $K$-invariant functions are induced from $H_y\simeq G_x$ acting on $C_{\mathrm{cts}}(V,M)$, with its possible rank-one sign. The equivariant section makes this the ordinary semilinear action on values together with the action on $V$. Its higher $H_y$-cohomology vanishes by the trace-element splitting. These induced neighborhoods cover the compact space $Y$. Choose a finite such cover and take successive differences of its $H$-invariant clopen members to obtain a disjoint finite invariant clopen partition. Each piece retains its local description and splitting. Finite additivity and finite-group Shapiro now prove <a href="#eq:cts-permutation-acyclic" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cts-permutation-acyclic">[eq:cts-permutation-acyclic]</a>.

Finally form the first-quadrant double complex $$C^u_{\mathrm{cts}}\bigl(G,\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_{k,\mathrm{cts}}(T_v,M)\bigr).$$ The compact $k$-linear contracting homotopy of the augmented $T_\bullet$ acts on these Hom modules: a continuous map from a compact domain into a step has image in a compact envelope, so integration and the contracting homotopy take place in complete steps by <a href="#lem:cts-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cts-comparison">4</a>. Computing first in the $v$ direction identifies the total cohomology with $H^*(G,M)$. Computing first in the $u$ direction and using <a href="#eq:cts-permutation-acyclic" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cts-permutation-acyclic">[eq:cts-permutation-acyclic]</a> leaves only $u=0$ and $0\leq v\leq a_Gd_G$. This proves the bound. Tensoring $M$ with $V$ preserves every step condition and the trace elements, so the same construction proves the last assertion with the identical bound. ◻

</details>

The preceding bound is deliberately larger than the dimension. It is its uniformity under finite twists that permits passage from torsion-free open subgroups to the full group, including at primes where $G$ has torsion.

<a id="stmt-prop-cts-full-duality"></a>
<div id="prop:cts-full-duality" class="proposition">

**Proposition 8** (Full-group duality). *Assume that the orientation character of $G$ is trivial over $k$. For every trace-admissible $M$ there are natural isomorphisms $$H_i(G,M)\simeq H^{d_G-i}(G,M)
                  \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z).$$ Here homology is zero in negative degrees, and cohomology is zero in negative degrees. In particular $H^j(G,M)=0$ for $j>d_G$. The ordinary stabilizer $P_n$ has trivial orientation character and $d_G=n^2$, so this assertion applies to it without a twist.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-cts-full-duality"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-cts-full-duality</summary>

<a id="eq:cts-bimodule-duality"></a>
*Proof.* Write $R=k[[G]]$, $R_K=k[[K]]$, $H=G/K$, and $\Sigma=k[H]$. Regard $\Sigma$ as the quotient bimodule of $R$. It is perfect as a left or right $R$-module, since it is induced from the length-$d_G$ free resolution over $R_K$. Uniform-group duality, with its conjugation action retained, gives $$\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}_R(\Sigma,R)\simeq\Sigma[-d_G]
 \label{eq:cts-bimodule-duality}$$ as a $(\Sigma,R)$-bimodule. To recall the equivariance in this formula, restrict $R$ to $R_K$ and decompose it into its finitely many cosets. The dual of the uniform resolution has cohomology only in degree $d_G$, with one orientation line on each coset. Right translation permutes those lines by the right regular action; precomposition by a quotient element gives the left regular action and its action on the orientation line. The latter is trivial by hypothesis. This proves exactly the two commuting actions asserted in <a href="#eq:cts-bimodule-duality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cts-bimodule-duality">[eq:cts-bimodule-duality]</a>. The uniform duality, orientation identification, and compatibility with conjugation are also recorded in Beaudry et al. (2022, Propositions 4.16 and 4.36, Theorem 4.19 and Remark 4.23) <a id="pm-cite-30"></a>[[bghs](#ref-bghs)].

Put $$C=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}_R(\Sigma,M)=\mathbf R\Gamma(K,M),\qquad
 B=\Sigma\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}M.$$ Perfectness permits evaluation of the dual resolution against $M$, so <a href="#eq:cts-bimodule-duality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cts-bimodule-duality">[eq:cts-bimodule-duality]</a> gives a natural equivalence $C\simeq B[-d_G]$ in the derived category of $\Sigma$-modules. The cohomology of $C$ lies in degrees $0,\ldots,d_G$. The finite free comparisons in <a href="#lem:cts-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:cts-comparison">4</a> show that these derived expressions compute precisely the specified continuous cochains and homology, even when $M$ is a union of steps.

<a id="eq:cts-finite-norm"></a>
We prove that the finite-group norm $$k\otimes_\Sigma^{\mathbf L}C
           \longrightarrow\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}_\Sigma(k,C)
       \label{eq:cts-finite-norm}$$ is an equivalence. This is the point where finite subgroup cohomology cannot be discarded. For any finite-dimensional left $\Sigma$-module $V$, derived adjunction gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ext}}^j_\Sigma(V,C)
       =H^j(G,V^*\otimes_kM).$$ By <a href="#prop:cts-isotropy-bound" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="prop:cts-isotropy-bound">7</a> these groups vanish for $j>a_Gd_G$, uniformly in $V$. Choose a bounded-below injective resolution $J^\bullet$ of $C$. If $N$ is greater than both $d_G$ and $a_Gd_G$, dimension shifting along its exact tail gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ext}}^1_\Sigma(V,\ker(J^N\to J^{N+1}))
       =\mathop{\mathrm{Ext}}^{N+1}_\Sigma(V,C)=0.$$ Every quotient $\Sigma/I$ by a left ideal is finite-dimensional. Baer’s criterion therefore says that this last kernel is injective. Truncating there gives a bounded complex of injective modules representing $C$.

For a finite group algebra, every injective module, including an infinite-dimensional one, is projective. Indeed, the canonical injection of any module $L$ into $\mathop{\mathrm{Hom}}_k(\Sigma,L)$ splits if $L$ is injective; the target is free because the symmetric pairing on $k[H]$ identifies coinduction with induction. On a free module of arbitrary rank the ordinary norm is an isomorphism from coinvariants to invariants: on each copy of $k[H]$ it sends the class of $1$ to $\sum_{h\in H}h$. It is consequently an isomorphism on projective summands. Applying this degreewise to the bounded injective-projective model of $C$ proves <a href="#eq:cts-finite-norm" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cts-finite-norm">[eq:cts-finite-norm]</a>, with no infinite totalization or completion.

The left-hand side of <a href="#eq:cts-finite-norm" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cts-finite-norm">[eq:cts-finite-norm]</a>, shifted by $d_G$, is $$(k\otimes_\Sigma^{\mathbf L}C)[d_G]
       \simeq k\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}M;$$ the right-hand side is $\mathbf R\Gamma(G,M)$. Taking cohomology in degree $-i$ of the shifted equivalence gives $H_i(G,M)=H^{d_G-i}(G,M)$, with the stated grading.

For $G=P_n$, its Lie algebra is the central division algebra $D_n$ of degree $n$ over $\mathbb Q_p$. Conjugation by $a\in D_n^\times$ has determinant $$\det(L_a)\det(R_a)^{-1}
   =\operatorname{Nrd}(a)^n\operatorname{Nrd}(a)^{-n}=1.$$ The orientation character is the reduction of this determinant character, hence is trivial. The dimension of $D_n$ is $n^2$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-auto-remark-1"></a>
<div class="remark">

**Remark 9**. For a nontrivial orientation character, the same proof retains its one-dimensional line in <a href="#eq:cts-bimodule-duality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:cts-bimodule-duality">[eq:cts-bimodule-duality]</a> and gives the corresponding orientation-twisted duality. We only use the untwisted case stated above. The proposition makes no assertion that arbitrary $k[[G]]$-modules have finite cohomological dimension: its trace-element hypothesis is essential when $G$ contains $p$-torsion.

</div>

<a id="sec:continuous"></a>
<a id="sec:independent-tuples"></a>
<a id="sec:laurent"></a>
<a id="sec:pro-transfer"></a>
<a id="part:tower"></a>
### Finite markings and the completed tower

<a id="sec:finite-markings"></a>
##### Finite markings and integral models

This section provides the finite algebraic data used by both sides of the proof. The whole models give coefficients whose boundary layers belong to the next height stratum; their localized summands give the marking covers whose completed tower is studied geometrically. We also identify the full division-point lift schemes, because later transfer maps require their scheme structure and natural group actions.

Fix a prime $p$ and a height $n$. Choose a finite field $k$ containing the fields of definition of the Honda groups $\Gamma_j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, and of their endomorphisms. We use Honda coordinates for which $[p]_{\Gamma_j}(T)=T^{p^j}$. In this section $$G=P_n,\qquad
 A_m=k[[u_m,\ldots,u_{n-1}]],\qquad 1\leq m\leq n.$$ The formal group $\mathcal F$ over $A_m$ is the restriction of the universal deformation of $\Gamma_n$ to the height-at-least-$m$ locus. The deformation-ring construction is due to Lubin and Tate (1966, Proposition 1.1 and Theorem 3.1) <a id="pm-cite-31"></a>[[lubinTate1966](#ref-lubinTate1966)]; the Honda conventions and endomorphism structure are recalled in Ravenel (1986, Appendix A2.2) <a id="pm-cite-32"></a>[[ravenel1986](#ref-ravenel1986)]. Its finite division schemes are formed over $A_m$ before any localization. If $m<n$, put $$x=u_m,\qquad B_m=A_m[1/x],\qquad r=n-m.$$ The chosen parameters are successive Hasse coefficients: the ideals of the deeper height loci are $(u_m,\ldots,u_{j-1})$, and the first coefficient of $[p]_{\mathcal F}(T)$ over $A_m$ is $xT^{p^m}$; compare Strauch (2007, (1.1) and §2) <a id="pm-cite-33"></a>[[strauch2007](#ref-strauch2007)]. Replacing a parameter by a unit multiple gives the same constructions.

<a id="eq:mark-height-character"></a>
The action of $G$ comes with coordinate changes $\alpha_g:g^*\mathcal F\longrightarrow\mathcal F$. Write $\chi_g=\alpha_g'(0)$ and let $\mathcal L_m$ denote the free rank-one $A_m$-module with this semilinear action. Composition of the $\alpha_g$ gives the cocycle identity for $\chi_g$. Comparing the leading coefficients of the $p$-series gives $$g(x)=\chi_g^{p^m-1}x.
 \label{eq:mark-height-character}$$ Thus $\mathcal L_m$ is the periodicity line, up to the immaterial choice of inverse convention. All its integer powers will be retained. All finite $A_m$-modules below carry their compact topology; localizations carry the bounded-denominator coefficient convention of <a href="#sec:continuous" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:continuous">2</a>.

<a id="pm-h-11"></a>
###### The coefficient class

Since the $p$-series factors through $T^{p^m}$, its $\ell$-fold iterate factors through $T^{p^{m\ell}}$. For $\ell\geq1$ and $0\leq b\leq m\ell$, define $$D_m(\ell,b)
   =A_m[\,T^{p^b}\,]\ \subseteq\
     A_m[[T]]/([p^\ell]_{\mathcal F}(T)).$$ The brackets here mean the $A_m$-subalgebra generated by the indicated element; it will be finite over $A_m$.

<a id="stmt-def-mark-coefficients"></a>
<div id="def:mark-coefficients" class="definition">

<a id="eq:mark-basic-coefficients"></a>
**Definition 10** (Allowed coefficients). The basic coefficients at height $m$ are $$\mathcal L_m^{\otimes w}\otimes_{A_m}
       \bigotimes_{j=1}^{s}D_m(\ell_j,b_j),
 \qquad w\in\mathbb Z,\quad 0\leq b_j\leq m\ell_j,
 \label{eq:mark-basic-coefficients}$$ where $s$ may be zero. These are functions on whole tuples of division points, with the indicated powered coordinates; no independence condition is imposed. The allowed class $\mathscr C_m$ is their closure under finite direct sums, tensor products, equivariant direct summands, and finite equivariant filtrations whose successive quotients belong to the class. An extension in this definition is an exact sequence of compact semilinear $A_m$-modules.

</div>

<a id="stmt-lem-mark-powered-division"></a>
<div id="lem:mark-powered-division" class="lemma">

**Lemma 11**. *The algebra $D_m(\ell,b)$ is finite free of rank $p^{n\ell-b}$ over $A_m$. Its construction and action are intrinsic to relative Frobenius and commute with restriction to a deeper height locus. Every member of $\mathscr C_m$ is finite free over $A_m$, and reduction modulo $x$ sends $\mathscr C_m$ into $\mathscr C_{m+1}$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-mark-powered-division"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-mark-powered-division</summary>

*Proof.* Write $[p^\ell]_{\mathcal F}(T)=f(T^{p^b})$. Modulo the maximal ideal of $A_m$, the series $f(Z)$ is $Z^{p^{n\ell-b}}$. Weierstrass preparation therefore gives $$f(Z)=v(Z)W(Z),\qquad
 W(Z)=Z^{p^{n\ell-b}}+\sum_{i<p^{n\ell-b}}c_iZ^i,$$ where $v$ is a unit and all $c_i$ lie in the maximal ideal. Consequently $[p^\ell](T)$ generates the same ideal as $W(T^{p^b})$. Division by this monic polynomial shows both that $A_m[Z]/(W(Z))\longrightarrow A_m[[T]]/([p^\ell](T))$, $Z\mapsto T^{p^b}$, is injective and that its image has basis $1,T^{p^b},\ldots,T^{p^b(p^{n\ell-b}-1)}$. This proves the rank assertion.

A coordinate change $T\mapsto a(T)$ carries $T^{p^b}$ to $a(T)^{p^b}$, a series in $T^{p^b}$. Thus the subalgebra is preserved; it is the relative Frobenius image of the division scheme on coordinate rings. The same monic-division calculation after base change identifies the resulting algebra with the corresponding powered division algebra of the restricted group. In particular it commutes with passage to $A_{m+1}=A_m/(x)$. The numerical restriction on $b$ persists, since $b\leq m\ell\leq(m+1)\ell$.

The basic modules are finite free. An extension with finite free quotient splits as an underlying $A_m$-module, so its middle term is finite free. A finite direct summand is projective and hence free over the local ring $A_m$. These facts also show that reduction modulo $x$ preserves the exact filtrations in the definition. The periodicity line restricts to the corresponding line at height $m+1$. The last assertion now follows by induction over the finite constructions defining the class. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-12"></a>
###### Connected jets and whole finite models

For the remainder of this section assume $m<n$. Over $B_m$, the connected part of $\mathcal F[p^\infty]$ is a formal group of height $m$. Its isomorphisms to $\Gamma_m$ form a pro-finite-étale $P_m$-torsor. The ring-level assertion used here is Lurie (2010, Lecture 14, Theorem 1) <a id="pm-cite-34"></a>[[lurieFormalGroups](#ref-lurieFormalGroups)]: the isomorphism algebra of two formal group laws of the same exact positive height over a ring is an increasing union of finite étale algebras. In the present Honda trivialization its finite quotients can be chosen as follows.

<a id="stmt-prop-mark-jets"></a>
<div id="prop:mark-jets" class="proposition">

<a id="eq:mark-jet-equations"></a>
**Proposition 12** (Integral connected-jet models). *For each $h\geq0$, the connected marking through exponent $p^h$ has a finite free model $H_{m,h}$ over $A_m$. There are coordinates $a_0,\ldots,a_h$ and polynomials in earlier coordinates such that $$\begin{aligned}
 a_0^{p^m-1}&=x,\\
 a_i^{p^m}-x^{p^i}a_i&=P_i(a_0,\ldots,a_{i-1}),
       &&1\leq i\leq h.
\end{aligned}
 \label{eq:mark-jet-equations}$$ If the first Hasse coefficient is normalized only up to a unit, the corresponding unit factors are inserted in these equations. The residue monomials $$a_0^{e_0}a_1^{e_1}\cdots a_h^{e_h},\qquad
 0\leq e_0<p^m-1,\quad 0\leq e_i<p^m\ (i>0),$$ are an $A_m$-basis. The $G$-action preserves this model and admits a finite filtration with quotients integer powers of $\mathcal L_m$. The filtration remains such a filtration on every deeper height locus.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-mark-jets"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-mark-jets</summary>

*Proof.* Write an isomorphism $f:\mathcal F\longrightarrow\Gamma_m$ as an ordinary power series. Its coefficient at $T^{p^i}$ is $a_i$. At a degree $j$ which is not a power of $p$, some intermediate binomial coefficient $\binom{j}{v}$ is nonzero modulo $p$. In the coefficient of $X^vY^{j-v}$ in $f(\mathcal F(X,Y))=\Gamma_m(f(X),f(Y))$, the unknown coefficient of $T^j$ therefore has a nonzero constant coefficient. All other terms involve earlier coefficients. It follows inductively that every non-$p$-power coefficient is a polynomial over $A_m$ in the preceding $a_i$.

Now compare $f([p]_{\mathcal F}(T))$ with $f(T)^{p^m}$. In degree $p^m$ this gives $a_0x=a_0^{p^m}$, hence the first equation, since $a_0$ is invertible on the open marking space. In degree $p^{m+i}$, the only term involving $a_i$ on the left is $x^{p^i}a_i$; all remaining terms involve earlier coefficients. This proves <a href="#eq:mark-jet-equations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="eq:mark-jet-equations">[eq:mark-jet-equations]</a>, with polynomials over $A_m$. The recursive comparison is also the usual proof of the Honda classification; see Ravenel (1986, Theorem A2.2.12, its proof, and Lemmas A2.2.20–A2.2.21) <a id="pm-cite-35"></a>[[ravenel1986](#ref-ravenel1986)].

Let $H_{m,h}$ be the successive monic algebra defined by these equations. Monic division gives the displayed basis, so it is finite free of rank $(p^m-1)p^{mh}$. After inverting $x$, $a_0$ is invertible, the derivative of its equation is invertible, and the derivative of the $i$th subsequent equation is $-x^{p^i}$. Thus $H_{m,h}[1/x]$ is finite étale.

The actual marking quotient is finite étale by the ring-level classification above. After a strictly henselian base change its fiber is the corresponding quotient of $P_m$. A Honda automorphism has $p^m-1$ possible nonzero linear coefficients, and $p^m$ choices at each succeeding $p$-power; the other coefficients are then determined. This follows either from the Honda coefficient calculation or from the order filtration on its endomorphism ring. Hence that quotient has rank $(p^m-1)p^{mh}$. The equations define a map from $H_{m,h}[1/x]$ to its coordinate ring. Every jet coefficient is a polynomial in $a_0,\ldots,a_h$, so these coordinates distinguish geometric jets. The map on geometric function algebras is therefore surjective, and finite étaleness gives surjectivity of the map itself. A surjection between finite étale algebras of the same rank is an isomorphism, as can be checked after strict henselization. This identifies the algebra, including over nonreduced test bases, with the connected marking quotient.

<a id="eq:mark-jet-triangular"></a>
Precomposing $f$ with $\alpha_g$ gives $$g(a_i)=\chi_g^{p^i}a_i+Q_{g,i}(a_0,\ldots,a_{i-1}),
 \qquad g(a_0)=\chi_ga_0.
 \label{eq:mark-jet-triangular}$$ Every coefficient in this formula lies in $A_m$; only finitely many coefficients of $\alpha_g$ are used at a fixed jet order. The formulas preserve the defining relations after inverting $x$. Since $H_{m,h}$ is $x$-torsion-free, they preserve them before localization as well. The inverse coordinate change supplies the inverse action.

Order the displayed basis lexicographically starting with $e_h$, then $e_{h-1}$, and so on. In expanding a transformed monomial, any use of an earlier-variable term in <a href="#eq:mark-jet-triangular" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="eq:mark-jet-triangular">[eq:mark-jet-triangular]</a> lowers this order. Reducing a power $a_i^{p^m}$ by its monic equation lowers it again. The diagonal term on a basis vector is therefore $\chi_g^{e_0+pe_1+\cdots+p^he_h}$. The initial spans in this order are stable, with the claimed line quotients. All these spans and quotients are free over $A_m$, so the filtration specializes exactly to every deeper height locus. Finally the formulas are continuous in $g$ and in the compact coefficient topology, because every fixed finite coefficient quotient uses finitely many coefficients of the continuous universal coordinate change. ◻

</details>

On the same open, marking the étale Tate module gives a $\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_r(\mathbb Z_p)$-torsor. Its action commutes with changes of connected marking and with $G$. Put $$J=P_m\times\mathop{\mathrm{GL}}_r(\mathbb Z_p).$$ We use a cofinal sequence of normal product congruence subgroups $U\subset J$. The connected factors can be chosen among the kernels of the jet quotients just constructed: the subsequence corresponding to $1+p^a\mathcal O_{D_m}$ is cofinal. After omitting finitely many terms, both factors, and hence $U$, are uniform and torsion-free. Let $B_U$ denote the finite étale $J/U$-torsor algebra of the two markings.

<a id="stmt-prop-mark-whole-model"></a>
<div id="prop:mark-whole-model" class="proposition">

**Proposition 13** (A whole model for a finite marking). *For each such $U$ there are a finite free $A_m$-algebra $A'$, with integral multiplication laws in a fixed basis, and a $G$-invariant idempotent $e\in B'=A'[1/x]$ such that $$B_U=eB',\qquad B'/B_m\text{ is finite \'{e}tale}.$$ As a semilinear $A_m$-module, $A'$ has a finite filtration whose quotients are basic coefficients in $\mathscr C_m$. Its reduction modulo $x$ has such a filtration in $\mathscr C_{m+1}$. In a whole basis $A'=\bigoplus_\nu A_m b_\nu$, the $G$-action is given by continuous matrices over $A_m$.
